claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 'Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?' and subclaim 'Does damage compound as edits accumulate?', run a realistic no-rollback sequential-edit benchmark. Use public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE edit sets on GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, applying ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and a simple in-context/IKE-style parameter-free baseline. Filter to facts recalled by the base model, then apply cumulative edit streams of 1, 10, 100, and 1000 edits without resetting weights. After each checkpoint, measure Reliability/Efficacy on edited prompts, Generalization/Paraphrase Score on equivalent prompts, Locality/Neighborhood Score on out-of-scope facts, perplexity on held-out text such as WikiText/LAMBADA, and downstream robustness on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions. Also include a rollback single-edit setting to reproduce the optimistic prior-work condition. If parameter editors maintain high reliability and generalization while preserving locality, perplexity, and robustness as edits accumulate, the main claim is weakened. If single-edit scores are high but sequential scores show falling locality, worsening perplexity, and degradation on unrelated tasks, this supports the claim that near-perfect results do not survive realistic evaluation and that damage compounds. If the parameter-free baseline has lower raw edit reliability but far better robustness and locality at large edit counts, it supports treating parameter-free editing as a serious alternative. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by existing public logs that report cumulative, no-rollback edit trajectories with the same editors, datasets, backbones, and unrelated-task robustness metrics, not only single-edit COUNTERFACT scores.

To address subclaim 'Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?' and subclaim 'Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model representation space?', measure the geometry of edit-induced perturbations. For each edited model from the first experiment, collect hidden states on a large public factual/text corpus, e.g. COUNTERFACT prompts plus WikiText or OpenWebText samples, and estimate per-layer representation covariance before editing. Decompose each layer into high- and low-variance principal directions, then quantify how much the activation change induced by ROME/MEMIT/MEND projects onto each eigenspace across edited, paraphrase, neighborhood, and unrelated prompts. Compare real edits to controls with matched Frobenius-norm random weight perturbations, same-layer constrained fine-tuning updates, and edits applied to alternative layers. Test whether low-variance projection ratio predicts locality loss, perplexity increase, or unrelated-task degradation after controlling for layer, edit norm, editor, model size, and edit count. If harmful edits consistently concentrate activation changes in low-variance directions and those projections predict damage better than edit norm or layer alone, this supports the geometric limitation claim. If damage is uncorrelated with eigenspectrum position and is explained by algorithm choice, layer choice, or excessive update norm, then the geometric claim is weakened. This could be made unnecessary by prior evidence that releases covariance spectra, edit-delta projections, matched perturbation controls, and regressions linking low-variance amplification to observed degradation across multiple models and editors.

To address subclaim 'Do localized weight edits propagate globally?' and subclaim 'Does a parameter-free approach leave the model weights untouched?', perform a propagation and intervention-localization study comparing weight-editing and parameter-free methods. On the same COUNTERFACT/ZSRE edits, record activation differences between the base and edited models across all layers, token positions, and prompt classes: edited prompts, paraphrases, semantically related neighbors, unrelated factual prompts, and general language prompts. Use causal tracing and an alternative representation-zeroing/restoration procedure to determine whether perturbations remain near the edited subject/layer or spread to distant tokens, later layers, and unrelated prompts. For parameter-free baselines such as IKE, SERAC-style retrieval if available, or prompt-memory editing, verify cryptographically or by tensor checksums that base-model weights are unchanged before and after editing, while separately accounting for extra memory or retrieved demonstrations. If parameter edits create measurable activation/logit shifts throughout the network and on unrelated prompts, while parameter-free methods leave weights unchanged and confine changes largely to prompts where memory is retrieved or evidence is prepended, this supports the global-propagation and parameter-free-alternative parts of the claim. If activation differences from parameter edits remain tightly localized and unrelated prompts are unaffected, the propagation claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released full-layer activation-difference maps and checksum-verified parameter-free baselines evaluated on the same public edit sets and prompt classes.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A clean pre-edit measurement and an explicitly non-teacher-forced single-edit evaluation that separate inference-protocol inflation from the effects of accumulating edits.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed benchmark includes a rollback single-edit condition, a no-rollback sequential condition, and a base-model recall filter, so it directly investigates single-versus-cumulative editing. However, it does not explicitly require scoring the unedited model as a measurement floor or specify plain autoregressive decoding for the single-edit comparison. The result could therefore conflate teacher-forcing/protocol effects with rollback and accumulation effects.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment isolates two possible explanations for optimistic results: an inflated inference protocol and the effects of editing repeatedly.
The proposed experiment includes realistic sequential editing and a rollback single-edit condition, so it reaches the same broad comparison.
It does not explicitly establish a clean score or require an autoregressive-versus-teacher-forced protocol comparison for the single-edit condition.
Consequently, a team could observe a single/sequential discrepancy without knowing whether the reference's protocol-inflation explanation is responsible.
The team would fail to learn cleanly what honest single-edit evaluation reveals independently of accumulation: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A semantic evaluation whose conclusions are independently checked by a deterministic token-level measure, allowing method rankings to be distinguished from artifacts of an automated judge.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments report reliability, efficacy, generalization, locality, perplexity, and downstream performance, but none specifies an independent token-level match-ratio/exact-match check against the semantic evaluation. Thus they do not validate that the editing-method ranking is robust to the scoring instrument.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment determines whether semantic-judge rankings are reproduced by a deterministic token-level measure.
The proposed set contains no such independent token-level cross-check or explicit judge-agreement analysis.
Any observed ranking could therefore still be an artifact of the chosen scoring procedure.
The team would fail to learn whether the reference's metric-validation result holds: missing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, variance-aware measurement of directional representation perturbations across edit counts, methods, and architectures, including whether low-variance directions show increasing relative amplification.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed geometry study measures covariance eigenspaces, compares low- and high-variance projections, uses matched perturbation controls, and tests edit-count and damage relationships across models and editors. That bears directly on the geometric explanation. But it describes projection amounts/ratios rather than an explicit variance-normalized directional change, so a low-variance subspace could appear prominent without demonstrating disproportionate amplification relative to its baseline variance.
reasoning_chain: The reference mechanism depends on relative change being large after normalization by the variance or singular value of each direction, not merely on the share of raw change lying in a subspace.
The proposed experiment estimates the variance spectrum and measures projections into low- and high-variance eigenspaces, with useful controls and accumulation points.
Its stated projection ratio does not specify normalization by the corresponding eigenvalues or an equivalent direction-specific relative-change statistic.
Therefore the experiment could find low-variance projection concentration while leaving the claimed amplification relation ambiguous.
The team would fail to determine decisively whether the proposed geometric mechanism is variance-normalized low-direction amplification: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A comparative, cumulative benchmark spanning multiple parameter-editing strategies, model backbones, factual-edit datasets, edit loads, and a parameter-free comparator, with measures of edit success, generalization, locality, and preservation of unrelated behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set supplies a cumulative no-rollback comparison at several edit counts on two factual-edit datasets and two large-model backbones, includes several distinct parameter-modifying strategies and a parameter-free baseline, and measures editing outcomes plus unrelated-task robustness. Experiment 2 adds the weight-untouched verification for the parameter-free arm. The exact method roster, models, datasets, and number of edit counts are not binding requirements of the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct post-edit evaluation of untargeted reasoning, knowledge, language, or other core capabilities at multiple accumulation levels, with enough unrelated tasks to reveal collateral damage rather than merely editing failure.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed benchmark evaluates held-out-text perplexity and unrelated downstream capabilities at the one, ten, one-hundred, and one-thousand-edit checkpoints, including the specifically relevant ten- and one-hundred-edit levels. These measurements can distinguish failure to edit facts from damage to capabilities outside the edited facts, even though the particular capability suites differ from the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the observed degradation is robust to model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or confidence, and editor configuration or architecture, rather than being an artifact of one experimental setting.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set uses two backbones, several editors, alternative layers, matched perturbation controls, and regressions controlling for model size, editor, layer, and edit count. It does not, however, run a larger-model sweep, an event-level knowledge condition, high/low-confidence fact splits, or a dedicated hyperparameter/configuration sensitivity analysis for a non-collapsing method. The generality of the collapse would therefore remain materially narrower and ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment tests whether the effect persists across scale, knowledge representation, fact difficulty, and sensitive method configurations.
The proposed set varies backbones and editors and controls for several experimental factors, so it provides some robustness evidence.
It does not vary the key knowledge type and confidence strata or perform the specified scale and configuration stress tests.
A collapse observed in the proposed set could still be caused by the selected fact format, difficulty distribution, model scale, or an untested configuration.
The team would fail to learn whether the limitation survives the full artifact-focused robustness sweep: partial.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests cumulative editing damage, untargeted capability loss, global propagation, and whether a parameter-free comparator changes the weights. It also substantially probes the geometric hypothesis. But it lacks an explicit clean-floor and decoding-protocol isolation, omits independent metric validation, does not state a variance-normalized directional amplification measure, and leaves scale/knowledge-type/confidence/configuration robustness unresolved. Those gaps prevent the full claim—including its protocol-independent empirical basis and geometric generality—from being settled as written.
missing: An explicit unedited baseline and a matched single-edit comparison under plain autoregressive decoding versus the teacher-forced protocol.
A deterministic token-level metric cross-check of the semantic editing scores.
A direction-specific change measure normalized by representation variance/singular value, with an explicit accumulation trend test.
Larger-model, event-level, fact-confidence/difficulty, and hyperparameter/architecture sensitivity sweeps.
